clue.text: A well-oiled lock?

parts.note: not a door fastening kept greased but a tuft of hair swept up and slicked down with brilliantine

explanation.surface: Someone praises a door fitting that turns smoothly thanks to regular oiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door, but it is a lock of hair; 'well-oiled' points to the greased styling of 1950s hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiff is a tuft of hair brushed up at the front, classically held in place with hair oil.

clue.text: Minimum investment for patrons of the pools!

definitions.text: Minimum investment for patrons of the pools!

parts.words: Minimum investment for patrons of the pools
parts.note: not the smallest stake in a football betting syndicate but the scantiest garment a swimmer could be dressed in

explanation.surface: A football-pools promoter advertises the lowest stake a punter may put in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The pools' suggests football pools betting, a British weekly gamble; here it means swimming pools, and 'investment' is punning on 'vestment', clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-piece swimsuit is about the least clothing a bather can wear, so it is the minimum 'in-vestment'.

clue.text: Genuine support for a team of stars

indicators.note: in a down entry the lower piece holds up the one placed above it

parts.note: a side is a team in sport
genuine means real

explanation.surface: A fan offers real backing to a side made up of star players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support for' works only because this is a down answer, where the lower piece stands beneath the upper one; 'stars' looks like star players but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidereal is the astronomers' adjective meaning relating to the stars, as in sidereal time.

clue.text: British Rail is going to Leatherhead and a city near Avon mouth

parts.note: BR is the abbreviation for British Rail, the old national railway
going to gives the short word to
the head of the word Leather is its first letter, L

explanation.surface: A railway timetable notice about a train service to Leatherhead, a Surrey town, and on to a West Country city.
explanation.walkthrough: Leatherhead is a real Surrey town, but here it is split: the 'head' of 'Leather' is L.
explanation.definitionFit: Bristol is the English port city standing on the River Avon a few miles from where it meets the Severn estuary.

clue.text: Seth runs round for Diana

indicators.note: round suggests turning the letters about, signalling a rearrangement of the preceding words

explanation.surface: A man called Seth goes jogging in circles for a woman named Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs' looks like the verb of the sentence, and 'round' like a jogging route, but both serve the rearrangement; Diana is the Roman hunting goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Diana was the Roman goddess of the hunt, the archetypal female hunter.

clue.text: William has an attempt at making butter

parts.note: Billy is a pet form of the name William
a go is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: A man named William tries his hand at churning butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the dairy spread but one who butts, as a male goat does with its horns.
explanation.definitionFit: A male goat is famous for ramming with its head, so it is a creature that butts.

clue.text: U. S. rifle is adapted for infantrymen

indicators.note: adapted means altered into a new form, signalling that the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters U and S taken as printed

explanation.surface: An American rifle has been modified for use by foot soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapted' rearranges the nine letters of U S RIFLE IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Fusiliers are soldiers of certain infantry regiments, originally armed with a light musket called a fusil.

clue.text: Port one gets in casks

indicators.note: gets in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: At a harbour, a single item is loaded among the barrels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets in' puts I inside TUNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunis, capital of Tunisia, is a Mediterranean seaport.

clue.text: Come up against an objection

parts.note: an gives the indefinite article A
a but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: Someone runs into a protest raised against their plans.
explanation.definitionFit: To abut is to border on or adjoin, meeting something along an edge.

clue.text: They lead in the forces if ordered

definitions.text: They lead in the forces if ordered

indicators.note: ordered means arranged afresh, signalling that the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Those in command of the armed services take charge when instructed to do so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges FORCES IF; the whole clue also describes the answer, so it is an all-in-one.
explanation.definitionFit: Commissioned leaders hold command over the ranks in the army, navy and air force.

clue.text: Dutch courage?

parts.note: boldness from alcohol, read as both the nerve itself (slang) and the container the drink comes in

explanation.surface: A query about bravery that comes from drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'bottle' means nerve or courage, and Dutch courage, liquor-fuelled bravery, comes out of one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for nerve, and drink-fuelled nerve is poured from a glass vessel.

clue.text: Drink we imbibe at home

indicators.note: imbibe means take in, so the word we takes the other piece inside it

parts.note: in means at home, as in 'staying in'

explanation.surface: A host offers a drink to be taken while staying in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imbibe' looks like drinking, chiming with the definition, but it is the container signal: the first-person plural pronoun swallows the word for being at home.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the drink made from fermented grapes.

clue.text: On balance it's depressing to do this

definitions.text: On balance it's depressing to do this

parts.words: On balance it's depressing to do this
parts.note: not gloomy overall but, on a pair of scales, pushing one pan lower by being the heavier

explanation.surface: Someone sighs that, all things considered, the task is a gloomy one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On balance' means 'overall' and 'depressing' means saddening on the surface; read literally, a heavier load on a balance depresses its pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Being heavier than something else makes your side of the scales go down.

clue.text: No beer left? That's the limit!

definitions.text: No beer left? That's the limit!

parts.words: No beer left? That's the limit
parts.note: not a drinker's complaint but a phrase for the very last point, with the last of the ale as a pun

explanation.surface: A pub-goer finds the barrel empty and declares it the final straw.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British style of beer, so the end of the bitter is no beer left; the phrase means the very last extremity.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the furthest point or very conclusion of something, however unpleasant.

clue.text: Rock 'n' roll player? The latter certainly

definitions.text: Rock 'n' roll player? The latter certainly

parts.words: Rock 'n' roll player? The latter certainly
parts.note: not a pop musician but a mechanical instrument that certainly plays perforated paper rolls

explanation.surface: A question whether someone performs rock and roll music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The latter' points to 'roll': the instrument is driven by punched paper rolls, whatever it may rock.
explanation.definitionFit: This self-playing piano works from perforated music rolls.

clue.text: Brown climbs mountains, making notes

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means going upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: tan is a brown colour
the Urals are a mountain range in Russia

explanation.surface: A man named Brown goes up mountains and takes notes on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbs' turns TAN upwards to NAT; 'Brown' looks like a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, a natural is a note neither sharpened nor flattened, or the sign cancelling a sharp or flat.

clue.text: Arrange a star part in a Western

definitions.meaning: to set people or things in order

definitions.text: a star part in a Western
definitions.meaning: the lawman role, a leading character in cowboy films

explanation.surface: A casting director sets up a leading role in a cowboy film.
explanation.definitionFit: To marshal is to arrange in order; a US marshal is a federal lawman, a classic lead in cowboy films.

clue.text: Surprise shots in a mé

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Surprise shots in a mé': the last word is cut short by OCR, so the anagram indicator after fodder SHOTS IN A is missing and no search gives it.

clue.text: This turns out to sum up Panama, for example

indicators.note: turns out suggests the letters are turned about into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone finds a calculation summarises things, citing Panama as an instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns out' rearranges THIS SUM; 'to sum up' reads as summarising, but 'to' and 'up' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Panama is a narrow strip of land joining two larger land masses, North and South America.

clue.text: Results of running repairs?

parts.note: both the sewn mending of a garment and the sharp side pains caused by running

explanation.surface: Someone asks what quick fixes made on the go have achieved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running repairs' means quick fixes; split, running gives side pains and repairs give sewn mends.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both the loops of thread in mending and the sudden cramps a runner gets.

clue.text: Worn tiles

parts.note: not roof slates gone shabby but tiles in the slang sense of headgear, which is worn

explanation.surface: A roofer points out tiles that have weathered and become shabby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tile' is old British slang for a hat; 'worn' means put on the head, not shabby.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiles is dated slang for headgear such as bowlers, and headgear is worn.

clue.text: What the sea may do to a ship

definitions.text: What the sea may do to a ship

parts.words: What the sea may do to a ship
parts.note: rough water throws a vessel about, pitching it up and down

explanation.surface: A question about how waves treat a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy waves throw a vessel about violently.

clue.text: He's too upset to calm down

indicators.note: upset means knocked over or disturbed, signalling that the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man is too agitated to settle himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges HES TOO; it looks like his emotional state.
explanation.definitionFit: To soothe is to calm or quieten someone who is agitated.

clue.text: Hard back

definitions.meaning: the rear part of a ship

explanation.surface: A two-word description of something firm at the rear.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern means strict or harsh, and it is also the rear end of a vessel.

clue.text: Where the Ark went fast

parts.note: the mountain on which Noah's vessel came to rest and stuck fast as the Flood receded

explanation.surface: A question about where Noah's vessel travelled at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went fast' suggests speed, but it means became stuck fast, as Noah's Ark ran aground on a mountain in the Book of Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis says Noah's vessel came to rest on the mountains of this peak in eastern Turkey.

clue.text: Keep for use as a hook?

definitions.meaning: a hook is something to suspend things from

explanation.surface: Someone decides to retain an object because it might serve as a peg.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means retain, and literally describes what a peg or hook lets you suspend things from.

clue.text: People pop in his shop

parts.note: not customers dropping by but people pawning goods with a pawnbroker, pop being slang for pawn

explanation.surface: Customers frequently drop into a relative's store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' is British slang for pawn, and 'uncle' is old slang for the pawnbroker, so 'pop in' means pawn goods rather than drop by.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker, to whom people take goods in exchange for a loan.

clue.text: Has insufficient funds and doesn't finish the course

definitions.meaning: covers less than the full distance of a race

explanation.surface: A runner out of cash fails to complete a race.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to have too little of something, and literally to cover less distance than required.
